title: Why do spellings go wrong a week after the test?
meta_description: A word spelled right on Friday can be wrong a week later because memory depends on how practice is spread across days. Here is what the research says.
hero_image_alt: Five blank cream index cards standing in a row along a white wooden shelf, with the gaps between them widening, and a sharpened navy pencil at the end.
content_html:
Spellings that were correct on Friday can be wrong a week later because how well a word is remembered depends on how practice was spread over time. A 2006 review of 317 experiments on verbal recall found that the gap between practice sessions and the delay before the final test operate jointly on how much is recalled. A single burst of practice close to the test uses only one of those gaps.

Key takeaways

  • A correct spelling on test day shows that the word was available on that day. It does not show the word will still be available next week.
  • A 2006 review of 317 experiments on remembering words and similar verbal material found that the best gap between practice sessions grows as the time until the final test grows.
  • In one 1985 study of 44 children in Grade 3, children who met four spelling words on an expanding schedule scored higher than children who met them back to back, although the final test came only one minute later.
  • No source read for this post tells a parent how many days apart to practise spellings, so the suggestions below are ways to try the idea, not a proven plan.

Why would a word that was right on Friday be wrong a week later?

A word can be right on Friday and wrong a week later because a test is a measurement taken at one moment, and memory for a word changes after that moment. The review of distributed practice published in Psychological Bulletin in 2006 treats the delay before the final test, called the retention interval, as part of the question. Its abstract says the gap between study sessions and the retention interval operate jointly to affect what is recalled at the final test.

For a parent, that means Friday’s score answers one question: could the word be written on Friday? It cannot answer the question that matters to a child’s writing, which is whether the word will be there in a story on the following Wednesday. That is reasoning from what the research measures, not a finding of its own.

Roediger and Karpicke, whose experiments are discussed in our post on why a child can spell a word at home but not in the test, found exactly this pattern. On a test given five minutes later, students who had restudied the material did better than students who had been tested on it, 81 per cent against 75. Two days later the order had reversed, 68 against 54, and after a week it had reversed further, 56 against 42. Their participants were university undergraduates, not children.

What does research say about spreading practice over several days?

Research on spreading practice, often called distributed or spaced practice, finds that the timing of practice sessions affects later recall, and that the best timing depends on how long the memory has to last. The 2006 review in Psychological Bulletin gathered 839 assessments of distributed practice from 317 experiments in 184 articles. It compared massed practice, where the same material is studied back to back, with spaced practice, where sessions are separated by a gap.

Its main finding, as the abstract puts it, is that the gap between sessions and the retention interval operate jointly, and that the gap producing the best retention increased as the retention interval increased. In plain terms, the further away the test is, the longer the useful gap between practice sessions.

That finding is about verbal recall tasks in general. The abstract does not say how many of the experiments involved children, does not mention spelling, and the record read for this post does not print the authors’ names. The review is best taken as a general account of how memory for words behaves, not as a spelling study.

Has anyone tested this with children and spelling?

A small number of studies have, and the one read in full for this post is Rea and Modigliani (1985), published in Human Learning. It involved 44 children from two Grade 3 classes at a school in British Columbia, with an average age of eight and a half. Each child learned to spell four words, brought, happily, machine and police, chosen because a pretest showed the children were not familiar with their spelling.

The children met each word on a schedule that either expanded the gaps between tests, with other material in between, or put the presentations and tests one after another. The oral test came one minute after the final presentation, with an untimed written test after it. On the oral test the expanded group averaged 90 per cent against 78 for the massed group, and on the written test 95 against 85. The authors report expanded practice as superior to massed practice, F(1, 36) = 4.55, p < 0.05.

Two limits are worth stating. The authors note that performance was close to the ceiling, ranging from 67 to 100 per cent correct, which leaves little room for a difference to show. And the study ran in one school, with four words and one short session, so it cannot show what happens over days or weeks, and it does not tell a parent how to space a school’s weekly list. What it does show is that an expanding schedule gave better results than a back to back one for eight year olds learning spellings in that setting.

What does that mean for a Monday to Friday routine?

A routine that returns to the same words on different days uses the spreading idea without adding time. These suggestions follow from the research above, and none of them is a method with proven results for spelling.

  • Split the list across days. Practise each word for a few minutes on two or three days, rather than all of them for twenty minutes on Thursday night.
  • Start each session with last session’s words. Ask the child to write them from memory before looking at anything. This follows the same reasoning as look, cover, write, check, where covering the word is the step that makes the child recall it.
  • Keep sessions short. Under ten minutes is a sensible target, because a short session is one a child will agree to repeat.
  • Return to Friday’s words once the test is over. Writing three or four of them from memory the following week is one way to find out which have stayed.

If the school sets a weekly list, the school’s words stay the school’s words. A parent is only deciding when to practise them. Our FAQ explains how Spelling Nest sits alongside a school’s list.

How can a parent tell whether a word has stuck?

A parent can tell whether a word has stuck by asking the child to spell it from sound, without clues, on a day that is not the day it was practised. A word right once, soon after practice, says little. A word right on separate days is stronger evidence, though no study read for this post sets the number of days that counts.

Three or four words checked cold at the start of the following week will usually tell a parent more than a second look at Friday’s score. If a word has gone wrong, that is useful information and not a failure: it marks the word to bring back sooner next time. The page on how spelling sticks sets out how this idea works.

Frequently asked questions

Is it normal for a child to forget spellings after the test?

It is normal for memory for a word to change after a test, and the research on spacing treats the delay after learning as part of the question. The 2006 review found that the delay before the final test affects how much is recalled and which gap between practice sessions works best.

How many days apart should spelling practice be?

The sources read for this post do not give a number of days for spelling. The 2006 review found that the best gap grows as the time until the test grows, but it covers verbal recall in general. Practising on two or three different days in a week is a reasonable thing to try.

Does this apply to younger children as well?

The evidence for younger children is mixed and not specific to spelling. A 2023 study of 167 preschoolers across three experiments, learning made up words during storybook reading, found that trying to recall the words gave no advantage over rereading after a five minute delay. The authors concluded that retrieval practice may only benefit young children under specific learning conditions. That study was about vocabulary and not spelling, so it shows that results from older students do not carry over automatically.

Does Spelling Nest use spaced practice?

Spelling Nest counts a word as mastered only when it has been spelled from sound, with no clues, on three different days. That is the app’s own definition of mastery and not a finding from the studies above.

If you would like short daily practice on the words your child’s school sets, Spelling Nest lets a family type in the list and work through it at spellingnest.co.uk/app.

Sources

  • "Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis", Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 354 to 380, May 2006. DOI 10.1037/0033-2909.132.3.354. Read via the PubMed record, which does not print the authors’ names, so they are not given here.
  • Rea, C. P. and Modigliani, V., "The Effect of Expanded versus Massed Practice on the Retention of Multiplication Facts and Spelling Lists", Human Learning 4, 11 to 18, 1985. Full text read on 13 November 2026.
  • Knabe, M. L., Bredemann, C. A. and Vlach, H. A., "A lack of retrieval practice effects in children’s recognition and recall memory of novel words during storybook reading", Frontiers in Developmental Psychology 1, 15 December 2023. DOI 10.3389/fdpys.2023.1270938. Read online.
  • Roediger, H. L. III and Karpicke, J. D., "Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention", Psychological Science 17(3), 249 to 255, 2006. Full text read on 13 November 2026.
